The text studies quivers with relations arising from non-commutative analogs of Jacobian ideals in the complete path algebra. In this setting, a quiver is considered together with a potential, and the relations are obtained by taking cyclic derivatives of that potential. This produces a natural class of algebras whose structure reflects both the combinatorics of the quiver and the algebraic information encoded in the potential.

Within this framework, the authors develop a representation-theoretic interpretation of quiver mutation at arbitrary vertices. Rather than treating mutation purely as a combinatorial operation on quivers, the theory explains how mutation acts on the corresponding categories of representations. This makes it possible to understand changes in the quiver in terms of transformations of modules over the associated algebras.

The approach substantially generalizes the classical Bernstein-Gelfand-Ponomarev reflection functors. Those functors describe how representations change under reflection at a sink or a source in an acyclic quiver. By contrast, the framework considered here applies to mutations at arbitrary vertices and allows for more general quivers, including those with relations determined by potentials. In this sense, it extends reflection functor techniques far beyond their original setting.

The work is motivated by several interconnected areas of mathematics and mathematical physics. Superpotentials arise naturally in physics, especially in the study of supersymmetric gauge theories, and lead to relations defined by cyclic derivatives. Calabi-Yau algebras provide an important homological context in which quivers with potential play a central role. Cluster algebras offer another major source of motivation, since quiver mutation is one of their fundamental operations. Together, these perspectives give the theory both its conceptual foundation and its broad range of applications.

The text develops a representation-theoretic framework for studying quivers with relations that arise from non-commutative analogs of Jacobian ideals in complete path algebras. Starting from a quiver, one considers its completed path algebra and imposes relations obtained from cyclic derivatives of a potential, or more generally from data behaving like a non-commutative Jacobian ideal. This point of view makes it possible to treat quivers with relations in a way that is compatible with the formalism of superpotentials and with the algebraic structures that appear in the theory of Calabi-Yau algebras.

A central goal of the text is to explain quiver mutation at an arbitrary vertex in representation-theoretic terms. Classical Bernstein-Gelfand-Ponomarev reflection functors describe how representations of a quiver change when one reflects at a sink or a source. However, ordinary reflection functors do not apply directly to mutation at a general vertex, since such a vertex may have both incoming and outgoing arrows and the mutation process also changes the relations. By working with complete path algebras and Jacobian-type ideals, the text constructs a broader setting in which mutation can still be interpreted as a transformation of representation categories.

In this generalized framework, mutation modifies not only the underlying quiver but also the associated relations. The resulting algebras retain enough structure to allow a meaningful comparison between their module categories. Thus, quiver mutation is not merely a combinatorial operation on arrows; it becomes a functorial or categorical process reflecting deeper algebraic behavior. In this sense, the theory extends the classical reflection functors of Bernstein, Gelfand, and Ponomarev from the special case of sinks and sources to the much wider context of arbitrary vertices in quivers with relations.

The discussion also connects the representation theory of quivers to several important areas of modern algebra and geometry. The use of potentials and cyclic derivatives places the subject in the setting of non-commutative geometry and superpotential algebras. These algebras often exhibit Calabi-Yau properties, which are central in the study of derived categories, Donaldson-Thomas theory, and mathematical physics. At the same time, quiver mutation is one of the fundamental operations underlying cluster algebras. By interpreting mutation representation-theoretically through Jacobian-type relations, the text helps clarify the relationship between cluster combinatorics, quiver representations, and Calabi-Yau algebraic structures.

Overall, the text presents quivers with potentials and their Jacobian algebras as a natural generalization of classical quiver representation theory. It shows that mutation at arbitrary vertices can be understood through an extension of reflection functor ideas, thereby linking the classical theory of quiver representations with contemporary developments in cluster algebras, superpotentials, and Calabi-Yau categories.

This text introduces two important mathematical ideas: the **Jacobian** and **Bernstein** polynomials.

The **Jacobian** is a matrix used in multivariable calculus to describe how a vector-valued function changes. If a function maps several input variables to several output variables, the Jacobian contains all first-order partial derivatives. It is especially useful in coordinate transformations, optimization, robotics, and differential equations. The determinant of the Jacobian can also show how areas or volumes change under a transformation.

**Bernstein** polynomials are another important concept in mathematics, especially in approximation theory and computer graphics. They are used to approximate continuous functions and form the basis of Bézier curves, which are widely used in design, animation, and typography. Bernstein polynomials are valued because they provide smooth and stable approximations.

This connection between the Jacobian and Bernstein methods can appear in numerical analysis and geometric modeling. For example, when studying a surface represented by Bernstein polynomials, the Jacobian can help analyze how the surface changes, bends, or transforms. Together, these tools support both theoretical mathematics and practical applications in science and engineering.

**Title:** Complete Path Algebras, Jacobian Ideals, and Quiver Mutation

This talk will introduce complete path algebras of quivers and the role of superpotentials in defining Jacobian ideals. These constructions provide a natural algebraic framework for studying quivers with relations, especially through the lens of noncommutative geometry and representation theory. We will discuss how quiver mutation acts on quivers with potential and how the associated Jacobian algebras behave under mutation. The talk will also highlight the motivation coming from cluster algebras, where quiver mutation is a fundamental combinatorial operation, and from physics-inspired superpotentials, which encode relations via cyclic derivatives. The goal is to explain how these ideas fit together and why complete path algebras and potentials are useful tools in modern algebra and geometry.
